# U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit – Civil Rights – Use of Deadly Force – Disability Discrimination
U.S. Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit

A mother could not pursue excessive force or disability discrimination claims arising from police shooting her mentally ill son after the Fourth Circuit concluded officers reasonably responded to an active shooter who repeatedly fired what appeared to be a real handgun during a neighborhood standoff.
The court affirmed summary judgment for the officers and the City of Charlotte, finding the use of deadly force was objectively reasonable under the Fourth Amendment and that police made reasonable efforts to accommodate the man’s mental illness under the Americans with Disabilities Act.
Affirming summary judgment, the Fourth Circuit held that the officers’ use of deadly force was objectively reasonable under the totality of the circumstances. The court stressed that officers are entitled to evaluate threats from the perspective of a reasonable officer on the scene rather than with hindsight. Morgan repeatedly ignored commands to drop the weapon, discharged it numerous times in a residential neighborhood, and appeared to present an immediate threat to officers and nearby residents.
Although the gun ultimately proved incapable of firing live ammunition, the court found it looked, sounded and functioned like an actual firearm, giving officers every reason to believe they faced an armed active shooter. The Fourth Amendment, the court explained, does not require officers to wait until they are certain a weapon is genuine before responding to an apparent deadly threat.
The ADA requires reasonable accommodations, the court said, not perfect ones, and it does not obligate officers to adopt alternative de-escalation strategies that would expose themselves or others to an immediate risk of serious harm.

- Anderson v. Liberty Lobby, Inc. and Fed. R. Civ. P. 56(a): Provide the materiality and genuineness framework for assessing whether disputes must go to a jury.

#### C. Fourth Amendment excessive force framework

- Graham v. Connor: Supplies the “objective reasonableness” standard and the familiar factors (severity of crime, immediate threat, resistance/flight).
- Tennessee v. Garner: Establishes the constitutional limits on deadly force against fleeing suspects: deadly force is unreasonable absent probable cause that the suspect poses a threat of serious physical harm, and “it is not better that all felony suspects die than that they escape.”

How they influenced the decision: Garner anchored the “bright line” principle the majority treated as clearly established in the relevant sense: deadly force is unjustified against a fleeing suspect who is not posing an imminent threat, even if suspected of a felony.

# Cooper v. Doyle (4th Cir. 2025)

The case concerns the fatal shooting of Kwamena Ocran by four Gaithersburg Police Department officers in January 2021. Ocran, who had recently been released from prison and was reported by a confidential informant to be armed, was surveilled by the officers after the informant indicated Ocran might attempt to sell a handgun. When Ocran left an apartment with the informant and was approached by the officers, he fled. The officers pursued him, and during the chase, multiple officers reported seeing a muzzle flash and believed Ocran fired a weapon in their direction. The officers collectively discharged 27 rounds, resulting in Ocran’s death. Forensic evidence revealed Ocran was shot multiple times in the back, and a handgun was found near his body, though no evidence indicated it had been fired.
After discovery, Melody Cooper, Ocran’s mother and personal representative, brought a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim alleging excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment. The United States District Court for the District of Maryland denied the officers’ motion for summary judgment and rejected their claim of qualified immunity, finding genuine disputes of material fact existed—particularly regarding whether Ocran pointed or fired his weapon at the officers. The court also denied the officers’ motion for reconsideration.
On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit dismissed the officers’ appeal to the extent it challenged the district court’s findings of disputed material facts, as such findings are not reviewable under the collateral order doctrine. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court’s ruling that, accepting the undisputed facts, the officers were not entitled to qualified immunity because the right to be free from deadly force when fleeing and not posing a significant threat was clearly established at the time of the incident. The case was remanded for further proceedings, including a jury trial.

Ocran, who had recently been released from prison and was reported by a confidential informant to be armed, was surveilled by the officers after the informant indicated Ocran might attempt to sell a handgun. When Ocran left an apartment with the informant and was approached by the officers, he fled. The officers pursued him, and during the chase, multiple officers reported seeing a muzzle flash and believed Ocran fired a weapon in their direction. The officers collectively discharged 27 rounds, resulting in Ocran’s death. Forensic evidence revealed Ocran was shot multiple times in the back, and a handgun was found near his body, though no evidence indicated it had been fired.

## 1. Introduction
This published Fourth Circuit decision arises from the January 8, 2021 fatal shooting of Kwamena Ocran by four Gaithersburg Police Department Street Crimes Unit officers—Officer James Doyle, Officer Kyle Khuen, Sgt. Willie Delgado, and Cpl.
Larbi Dakkouni.

seltz.snippet:
> An officer doesn’t get to manufacture a deadly-force justification by placing themselves in the vehicle’s path when the car isn’t presenting an unavoidable, imminent threat. ADAMS V SPEERS

*Tennessee v. Garner* established the foundational rule: **An officer cannot use deadly force against a fleeing suspect who is unarmed and not dangerous**[1]. Deadly force is only justified if it is **necessary to prevent escape** **and** the officer has **probable cause** to believe the suspect poses an **immediate threat of death or serious injury** to officers or others[1]. In Garner, police shot a burglar running away; the Court struck down a state law allowing such force, holding that **“an officer may not seize an unarmed, nondangerous suspect by shooting him dead”**[1]. This Fourth Amendment rule (often called the “fleeing felon” rule) underpins all later cases: **flight alone does not justify deadly force** unless a severe, imminent threat exists[2].

- **Gonzalez v. City of Anaheim** (9th Cir. 2014) – Two officers stopped Adolph Gonzalez, who tried to drive off. One officer ended up partially inside Gonzalez’s van and fatally shot him in the head. The Ninth Circuit (en banc) *reversed* summary judgment for the officers, finding factual disputes about danger. The officers’ stories conflicted on whether the van was **rapidly accelerating** and posing an **immediate threat** when the shot was fired[3]. Because a jury could find the van was merely being used to escape (not as a weapon), deadly force might be *unreasonable*. The court emphasized that if the officer was not actually in imminent peril, shooting a fleeing driver would violate the Fourth Amendment[3]. ultimate.snippet:
# Cooper v. Doyle (4th Cir. 2025)

The case concerns the fatal shooting of Kwamena Ocran by four Gaithersburg Police Department officers in January 2021. Ocran, who had recently been released from prison and was reported by a confidential informant to be armed, was surveilled by the officers after the informant indicated Ocran might attempt to sell a handgun. When Ocran left an apartment with the informant and was approached by the officers, he fled. The officers pursued him, and during the chase, multiple officers reported seeing a muzzle flash and believed Ocran fired a weapon in their direction. The officers collectively discharged 27 rounds, resulting in Ocran’s death. Forensic evidence revealed Ocran was shot multiple times in the back, and a handgun was found near his body, though no evidence indicated it had been fired.
After discovery, Melody Cooper, Ocran’s mother and personal representative, brought a 42 U.S.C. § 1983 claim alleging excessive force in violation of the Fourth Amendment. The United States District Court for the District of Maryland denied the officers’ motion for summary judgment and rejected their claim of qualified immunity, finding genuine disputes of material fact existed—particularly regarding whether Ocran pointed or fired his weapon at the officers. The court also denied the officers’ motion for reconsideration.
On appeal, the United States Court of Appeals for the Fourth Circuit dismissed the officers’ appeal to the extent it challenged the district court’s findings of disputed material facts, as such findings are not reviewable under the collateral order doctrine. The Fourth Circuit affirmed the district court’s ruling that, accepting the undisputed facts, the officers were not entitled to qualified immunity because the right to be free from deadly force when fleeing and not posing a significant threat was clearly established at the time of the incident. The case was remanded for further proceedings, including a jury trial.
